Main.sentence: Saudi Arabia , [d] officially the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia ( KSA ), [e] is a country in ___E:West Asia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Asia)___ .

Located in the center of the ___E:Middle East U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_East)___ , it covers the bulk of the ___E:Arabian Peninsula U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabian_Peninsula)___ and has a land area of about 2,150,000 km 2 (830,000 sq mi), making it the ___E:fifth-largest country U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Asian_countries_by_area)___ in ___E:Asia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asia)___ , the largest in the Middle East, and the ___E:twelfth-largest U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_and_dependencies_by_area)___ in the world.

It is bordered by the ___E:Red Sea U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Sea)___ to the west; ___E:Jordan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jordan)___ , ___E:Iraq U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iraq)___ , and ___E:Kuwait U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kuwait)___ to the north; the ___E:Persian Gulf U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persian_Gulf)___ , ___E:Bahrain U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bahrain)___ , ___E:Qatar U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qatar)___ and the ___E:United Arab Emirates U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates)___ to the east; ___E:Oman U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oman)___ to the southeast; and ___E:Yemen U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yemen)___ to ___E:the south U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi_Arabia%E2%80%93Yemen_border)___ .

The ___E:Gulf of Aqaba U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_of_Aqaba)___ in the northwest separates Saudi Arabia from ___E:Egypt U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egypt)___ and ___E:Israel U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel)___ .
Saudi Arabia is the only country with a coastline along both the Red Sea and the Persian Gulf, and most of its terrain consists of arid desert, lowland, steppe, and mountains.

The capital and largest city is ___E:Riyadh U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riyadh)___ ; other major cities include ___E:Jeddah U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeddah)___ and the two holiest cities in ___E:Islam U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islam)___ , ___E:Mecca U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca)___ and ___E:Medina U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medina)___ .
With a population of almost 32.2 million, Saudi Arabia is the fourth most populous country in the ___E:Arab world U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arab_world)___ .

___E:Pre-Islamic Arabia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pre-Islamic_Arabia)___ , the territory that constitutes modern-day Saudi Arabia, was the site of several ancient cultures and civilizations; the ___E:prehistory of Saudi Arabia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Saudi_Arabia#Pre-Islamic_Arabia)___ shows some of the earliest traces of human activity outside ___E:Africa U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Africa)___ .  ___E:Islam U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islam)___ , the world's second-largest religion,  emerged in what is now Saudi Arabia in the early ___E:seventh century U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/7th_century)___ .

Islamic prophet ___E:Muhammad U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad)___ united the population of the ___E:Arabian Peninsula U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabian_Peninsula)___ and created a single Islamic religious polity.

Following his death in 632, his followers expanded Muslim rule beyond Arabia, ___E:conquering U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_Muslim_conquests)___ territories in ___E:North Africa U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Africa)___ , ___E:Central U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Asia)___ , ___E:South Asia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Asia)___ and ___E:Iberia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iberian_Peninsula)___ within decades.

Arab dynasties originating from modern-day Saudi Arabia founded the ___E:Rashidun U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rashidun_Caliphate)___ (632–661), ___E:Umayyad U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umayyad_Caliphate)___ (661–750), ___E:Abbasid U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbasid_Caliphate)___ (750–1517), and ___E:Fatimid U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fatimid_Caliphate)___ (909–1171) caliphates, as well as ___E:numerous other Muslim states U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Muslim_states_and_dynasties)___ in Asia, ___E:Africa U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islam_in_Africa#History)___ , and ___E:Europe U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islam_in_Europe#Western_Europe_and_the_Mediterranean_Region)___ .

Saudi Arabia was founded in 1932 by ___E:King Abdulaziz U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ibn_Saud)___ (also known as Ibn Saud), who united the regions of ___E:Hejaz U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hejaz)___ , ___E:Najd U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Najd)___ , parts of ___E:Eastern Arabia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Arabia)___ (Al-Ahsa) and ___E:South Arabia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Arabia)___ ( ___E:Asir U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asir)___ ) into a single state through ___E:a series of military and political campaigns U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unification_of_Saudi_Arabia)___ beginning in 1901. The country has since been governed as an ___E:absolute monarchy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Absolute_monarchy)___ under the ___E:House of Saud U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Saud)___ .

In its ___E:Basic Law U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basic_Law_of_Saudi_Arabia)___ , Saudi Arabia defines itself as a sovereign Arab ___E:Islamic state U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_state)___ with ___E:Islam as its official religion U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islam_in_Saudi_Arabia)___ and ___E:Arabic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabic)___ as its official language.

The ultraconservative ___E:Wahhabi U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wahhabism)___ religious movement within ___E:Sunni Islam U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunni_Islam)___ was the prevailing political and cultural force until the 2000s.

The Saudi government has attracted criticism for various policies such as its ___E:intervention in the Yemeni Civil War U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi-led_intervention_in_the_Yemeni_civil_war)___ , restrictions on political and civil liberties, and poor ___E:human rights record U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_rights_in_Saudi_Arabia)___ .
Since the mid-2010s, Saudi Arabia has instituted limited and gradual reforms to liberalize social, cultural, and religious life.
Saudi Arabia is considered both a ___E:regional U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regional_power)___ and ___E:middle U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_power)___ power.

Since ___E:petroleum U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petroleum)___ was ___E:discovered in the country in 1938 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dammam_No._7)___ ,   the kingdom has become the world's ___E:second-largest oil producer U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_oil_production)___ and leading ___E:oil exporter U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_oil_exports)___ , controlling the world's ___E:second-largest oil reserves U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_proven_oil_reserves#Countries)___ and ___E:sixth-largest gas reserves U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_natural_gas_proven_reserves)___ .

Saudi Arabia is categorized as a ___E:World Bank high-income economy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Bank_high-income_economy)___ and is the only Arab country among the ___E:G20 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G20)___ major economies.

The ___E:Saudi economy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Saudi_Arabia)___ is the ___E:largest in the Middle East U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_the_Middle_East)___ and the world's ___E:nineteenth-largest by nominal GDP U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_GDP_(nominal))___ and ___E:seventeenth-largest by PPP U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_GDP_(PPP))___ .

Ranking very high in the ___E:Human Development Index U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_Development_Index)___ ,  Saudi Arabia offers ___E:free university tuition U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Higher_education_in_Saudi_Arabia)___ , no personal income tax,  and ___E:free universal health care U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Health_care_in_Saudi_Arabia)___ .

With its ___E:dependence on foreign labour U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign_workers_in_Saudi_Arabia)___ , Saudi Arabia has the world's ___E:third-largest immigrant population U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_sovereign_states_by_immigrant_and_emigrant_population)___ , with foreign-born residents comprising roughly 40% of the population.  ___E:Saudi Arabians U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudis)___ are among ___E:the world's youngest people U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Youth_in_Saudi_Arabia)___ , with approximately half being under 25 years old.   Saudi Arabia is a member of the ___E:Gulf Cooperation Council U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_Cooperation_Council)___ , ___E:United Nations U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations)___ , ___E:Organisation of Islamic Cooperation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organisation_of_Islamic_Cooperation)___ , ___E:Arab League U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arab_League)___ , and ___E:OPEC U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OPEC)___ , as well as a dialogue partner of the ___E:Shanghai Cooperation Organisation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shanghai_Cooperation_Organisation)___ .

Following the amalgamation of the ___E:Kingdom of Hejaz U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Hejaz)___ and ___E:Nejd U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sultanate_of_Nejd)___ , ___E:Abdulaziz U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ibn_Saud)___ issued a royal decree on 23 September 1932 naming the new state al-Mamlaka al-ʿArabiyya as-Suʿūdiyya ( ___E:Arabic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabic)___ المملكة العربية السعودية ), which is normally translated as "the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia" in English,  but literally means "the Saudi Arab Kingdom ",  or "the Saudi Kingdom of Arabia " (compare ___E:the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hashemite_Kingdom_of_Jordan)___ ).

The word "Saudi" is derived from the element as-Suʿūdīyya in the Arabic name of the country, which is a type of adjective known as a nisba, formed from the dynastic name of the Saudi royal family, the ___E:Al Saud U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Saud)___ ( ___E:Arabic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabic_language)___ : آل سعود ).
Its inclusion expresses the view that the country is the personal possession of the royal family.
Al Saud is an ___E:Arabic name U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabic_name)___ formed by adding the word Al , meaning "family of" or "House of",  to the personal name of an ancestor.

In the case of Al Saud, this is ___E:Saud ibn Muhammad ibn Muqrin U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saud_ibn_Muhammad_ibn_Muqrin)___ , the father of the dynasty's 18th-century founder, ___E:Muhammad bin Saud U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_bin_Saud)___ .

There is evidence that human habitation in the ___E:Arabian Peninsula U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabian_Peninsula)___ dates back to about 125,000 years ago.  A 2011 study found that the first modern humans to spread east across Asia left ___E:Africa U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Africa)___ about 75,000 years ago across the ___E:Bab-el-Mandeb U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bab-el-Mandeb)___ connecting the ___E:Horn of Africa U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horn_of_Africa)___ and Arabia.
The Arabian Peninsula is regarded as central to the understanding of evolution and dispersals of humanity.
Arabia underwent an extreme environmental fluctuation in the ___E:Quaternary U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quaternary)___ that led to profound evolutionary and demographic changes.

Arabia has a rich ___E:Lower Paleolithic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lower_Paleolithic)___ record, and the quantity of ___E:Oldowan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oldowan)___ -like sites in the region indicate a significant role that Arabia had played in the early hominin colonization of Eurasia.

In the ___E:Neolithic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neolithic)___ period, prominent cultures such as ___E:Al-Magar U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Magar)___ , whose centre lay in modern-day southwestern Najd, flourished.
Al-Magar could be considered a "Neolithic Revolution" in human knowledge and handicraft skills.
The culture is characterized as being one of the world's first to involve the widespread domestication of animals, particularly the horse, during the Neolithic period.
Al-Magar statues were made from local stone, and it seems that the statues were fixed in a central building that might have had a significant role in the social and religious life of the inhabitants.

In November 2017, hunting scenes showing images of most likely domesticated dogs (resembling the ___E:Canaan Dog U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canaan_Dog)___ ) and wearing leashes were discovered in Shuwaymis, a hilly region of northwestern Saudi Arabia.
These rock engravings date back more than 8000 years, making them the earliest depictions of dogs in the world.

At the end of the 4th millennium BC, Arabia entered the ___E:Bronze Age U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bronze_Age)___ ; metals were widely used, and the period was characterized by its 2 m high burials which were simultaneously followed by the existence of numerous temples that included many free-standing sculptures originally painted with red colours.

In May 2021, archaeologists announced that a 350,000-year-old ___E:Acheulean U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acheulean)___ site named An Nasim in the ___E:Hail region U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E1%B8%A4a%CA%BCil_Province)___ could be the oldest human habitation site in northern Saudi Arabia. 354 artefacts, including hand axes and stone tools, provided information about the tool-making traditions of the earliest living man who inhabited southwest Asia. ___E:Paleolithic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paleolithic)___ artefacts are similar to material remains uncovered at the Acheulean sites in the ___E:Nefud Desert U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An_Nafud)___ .
The earliest sedentary culture in Saudi Arabia dates back to the ___E:Ubaid period U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ubaid_period)___ at ___E:Dosariyah U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dosariyah)___ .
Climatic change and the onset of aridity may have brought about the end of this phase of settlement, as little archaeological evidence exists from the succeeding millennium.
The settlement of the region picks up again in the period of ___E:Dilmun U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dilmun)___ in the early 3rd millennium.

Known records from ___E:Uruk U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uruk)___ refer to a place called Dilmun, associated on several occasions with copper, and in later periods it was a source of imported woods in southern Mesopotamia.

Scholars have suggested that Dilmun originally designated the ___E:Eastern Province U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Province,_Saudi_Arabia)___ , notably linked with the major Dilmunite settlements of Umm an-Nussi and Umm ar-Ramadh in the interior and Tarout on the coast.
It is likely that ___E:Tarout Island U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tarout_Island)___ was the main port and the capital of Dilmun.
Mesopotamian inscribed clay tablets suggest that, in the early period of Dilmun, a form of hierarchical organized political structure existed.
In 1966, an earthwork in Tarout exposed an ancient burial field that yielded a large statue dating to the Dilmunite period (mid 3rd millennium BC).
The statue was locally made under the strong Mesopotamian influence on the artistic principle of Dilmun.

By 2200 BC, the centre of Dilmun shifted for unknown reasons from Tarout and the Saudi Arabian mainland to the island of Bahrain, and a highly developed settlement emerged there, where a laborious temple complex and thousands of burial mounds dating to this period were discovered.

By the late ___E:Bronze Age U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bronze_Age)___ , a historically recorded people and land ( ___E:Midian U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midian)___ and the Midianites) in the north-western portion of Saudi Arabia are well-documented in the Bible.

Centred in ___E:Tabouk U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tabuk,_Saudi_Arabia)___ , it stretched from ___E:Wadi Arabah U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wadi_Arabah)___ in the north to the area of al-Wejh in the south.
The capital of Midian was Qurayyah,  it consists of a large, fortified citadel encompassing 35 hectares and below it lies a walled settlement of 15 hectares.
The city hosted as many as 12,000 inhabitants.

The Bible recounts ___E:Israel U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Israel_(united_monarchy))___ 's ___E:two wars U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midian_war)___ with Midian, somewhere in the early 11th century BC. Politically, the Midianites were described as having a decentralized structure headed by five kings (Evi, Rekem, Tsur, Hur, and Reba); the names appear to be toponyms of important Midianite settlements.

It is common to view that Midian designated a confederation of tribes, the sedentary element settled in the Hijaz while its nomadic affiliates pastured and sometimes pillaged as far away as ___E:Palestine U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palestine_(region))___ .

The nomadic ___E:Midianites U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midianites)___ were one of the earliest exploiters of the domestication of camels that enabled them to navigate through the harsh terrains of the region.
At the end of the 7th century BC, an emerging kingdom appeared in north-western Arabia.
It started as a sheikdom of Dedan, which developed into the kingdom of ___E:Lihyan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lihyan)___ .
During this period, Dedan transformed into a kingdom that encompassed a much wider domain.

In the early 3rd century BC, with bustling economic activity between the south and north, Lihyan acquired large influence suitable to its strategic position on the caravan road.  The Lihyanites ruled over a large domain from ___E:Yathrib U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medina)___ in the south and parts of the Levant in the north.
In antiquity, Gulf of Aqaba used to be called Gulf of Lihyan, a testimony to the extensive influence that Lihyan acquired.

The Lihyanites fell into the hands of the ___E:Nabataeans U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nabataeans)___ around 65 BC upon their seizure of Hegra then marching to ___E:Tayma U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tayma)___ , and to their capital Dedan in 9 BC. The Nabataeans ruled large portions of north Arabia until their domain was annexed by the ___E:Roman Empire U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Empire)___ , which renamed it ___E:Arabia Petraea U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabia_Petraea)___ , and remained under the rule of the Romans until 630.
Shortly before the advent of Islam, apart from urban trading settlements (such as Mecca and Medina), much of what was to become Saudi Arabia was populated by nomadic pastoral tribal societies.
The Islamic prophet Muhammad was born in Mecca in about 570 ___E:CE U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_Era)___ .

In the early 7th century, ___E:Muhammad U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad)___ united the ___E:various tribes of the peninsula U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tribes_of_Arabia)___ and created a single Islamic religious polity.

Following his death in 632, his followers expanded the territory under Muslim rule beyond Arabia, conquering territory in the Iberian Peninsula in the west, to parts of Central and South Asia in the east, in a matter of decades.
Arabia became a more politically peripheral region of the Muslim world as the focus shifted to the newly conquered lands.

___E:Arabs U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arab)___ originating from modern-day Saudi Arabia, the ___E:Hejaz U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hejaz)___ in particular, founded the ___E:Rashidun U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rashidun_Caliphate)___ (632–661), ___E:Umayyad U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umayyad_Caliphate)___ (661–750), ___E:Abbasid U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbasid_Caliphate)___ (750–1517), and the ___E:Fatimid U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fatimid_Caliphate)___ (909–1171) caliphates.

From the 10th century to the early 20th century, Mecca and Medina were under the control of a local Arab ruler known as the ___E:Sharif of Mecca U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sharif_of_Mecca)___ , but at most times the Sharif owed allegiance to the ruler of one of the major Islamic empires based in ___E:Baghdad U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baghdad)___ , ___E:Cairo U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cairo)___ or ___E:Istanbul U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul)___ .
Most of the remainder of what became Saudi Arabia reverted to traditional tribal rule.

For much of the 10th century, the ___E:Isma'ili U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isma%27ilism)___ -Shi'ite ___E:Qarmatians U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qarmatians)___ were the most powerful force in the Persian Gulf. In 930, the Qarmatians pillaged Mecca, outraging the Muslim world, particularly with their theft of the ___E:Black Stone U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Stone)___ .

In 1077–1078, an Arab sheikh named ___E:Abdullah bin Ali Al Uyuni U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abdullah_bin_Ali_Al_Uyuni)___ defeated the Qarmatians in ___E:Bahrain U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Arabia)___ and ___E:al-Hasa U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Ahsa_Oasis)___ with the help of the ___E:Seljuq Empire U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seljuk_Empire)___ and founded the ___E:Uyunid dynasty U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uyunid_dynasty)___ .

The ___E:Uyunid Emirate U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uyunid_Emirate)___ later underwent expansion, with its territory stretching from Najd to the ___E:Syrian Desert U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syrian_Desert)___ .

They were overthrown by the ___E:Usfurids U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Usfurids)___ in 1253.  Usfurid rule was weakened after Persian rulers of ___E:Hormuz U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ormus)___ captured Bahrain and ___E:Qatif U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qatif)___ in 1320.  The vassals of Ormuz, the Shia ___E:Jarwanid dynasty U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jarwanid_dynasty)___ came to rule eastern Arabia in the 14th century.

The ___E:Jabrids U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jabrids)___ took control of the region after overthrowing the Jarwanids in the 15th century and clashed with Hormuz for more than two decades over the region for its economic revenues, until finally agreeing to pay ___E:tribute U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tribute)___ in 1507.  ___E:Al-Muntafiq U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Muntafiq)___ tribe later took over the region and came under ___E:Ottoman U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_Empire)___ ___E:suzerainty U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suzerainty)___ .
The ___E:Bani Khalid tribe U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bani_Khalid_(tribe))___ later revolted against them in the 17th century and took control.
Their rule extended from Iraq to Oman at its height, and they too came under Ottoman suzerainty.

In the 16th century, the Ottomans added the Red Sea and Persian Gulf coast (the Hejaz, ___E:Aseer U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aseer)___ and ___E:Al-Ahsa U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Arabia)___ ) to the empire and claimed suzerainty over the interior.

One reason was to ___E:thwart Portuguese attempts U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman%E2%80%93Portuguese_conflicts_(1538%E2%80%931560))___ to attack the Red Sea (hence the Hejaz) and the Indian Ocean.
The Ottoman degree of control over these lands varied over the next four centuries with the fluctuating strength or weakness of the empire's central authority.

These changes contributed to later uncertainties, such as the dispute with Transjordan over the ___E:inclusion of the sanjak of Ma'an U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Occupation_of_Ma%27an)___ , including the cities of ___E:Ma'an U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ma%27an)___ and ___E:Aqaba U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aqaba)___ .

The emergence of what was to become the Saudi royal family, known as the Al Saud, began at the town of ___E:Diriyah U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diriyah)___ in ___E:Nejd U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nejd)___ in central Arabia with the accession as ___E:emir U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emir)___ of ___E:Muhammad bin Saud U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_bin_Saud)___ on 22 February 1727.   In 1744 he joined forces with the religious leader ___E:Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_ibn_Abd_al-Wahhab)___ ,  founder of the Wahhabi movement, a strict puritanical form of Sunni Islam.
This alliance provided the ideological impetus to Saudi expansion and remains the basis of Saudi Arabian dynastic rule today.

The ___E:Emirate of Diriyah U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emirate_of_Diriyah)___ established in the area around Riyadh rapidly expanded and briefly controlled most of the present-day territory of Saudi Arabia, ___E:sacking Karbala U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wahhabi_sack_of_Karbala)___ in 1802, and ___E:capturing Mecca U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Destruction_of_early_Islamic_heritage_sites_in_Saudi_Arabia)___ in 1803. In 1818, it was destroyed by the Ottoman viceroy of Egypt, ___E:Mohammed Ali Pasha U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Ali_of_Egypt)___ .

The much smaller ___E:Emirate of Nejd U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emirate_of_Nejd)___ was established in 1824. Throughout the rest of the 19th century, the Al Saud contested control of the interior of what was to become Saudi Arabia with another Arabian ruling family, the ___E:Al Rashid U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rashidi_dynasty)___ , who ruled the ___E:Emirate of Jabal Shammar U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emirate_of_Jabal_Shammar)___ .
By 1891, the Al Rashid were victorious and the Al Saud were driven into exile in Kuwait.
At the beginning of the 20th century, the Ottoman Empire continued to control or have a suzerainty over most of the peninsula.

Subject to this suzerainty, Arabia was ruled by a patchwork of tribal rulers,   with the ___E:Sharif of Mecca U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sharif_of_Mecca)___ having pre-eminence and ruling the Hejaz.

In 1902, ___E:Abdul Rahman U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abdul_Rahman_bin_Faisal)___ 's son, Abdulaziz—later known as ___E:Ibn Saud U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ibn_Saud)___ —recaptured control of Riyadh bringing the Al Saud back to Nejd, creating the ___E:third "Saudi state" U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emirate_of_Nejd_and_Hasa)___ .

Ibn Saud gained the support of the ___E:Ikhwan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ikhwan)___ , a tribal army inspired by Wahhabism and led by ___E:Faisal Al-Dawish U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_Al-Dawish)___ , and which had grown quickly after its foundation in 1912.  With the aid of the Ikhwan, Ibn Saud captured Al-Ahsa from the Ottomans in 1913.

In 1916, with the encouragement and support of ___E:Britain U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom_of_Great_Britain_and_Ireland)___ (which was fighting the Ottomans in ___E:World War I U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I)___ ), the Sharif of Mecca, ___E:Hussein bin Ali U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hussein_bin_Ali,_Sharif_of_Mecca)___ , led a pan- ___E:Arab Revolt U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arab_Revolt)___ against the Ottoman Empire to create a united Arab state.

Although the revolt failed in its objective, ___E:the Allied U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allies_of_World_War_I)___ victory in World War I resulted in the end of Ottoman suzerainty and control in Arabia, and Hussein bin Ali became ___E:King of Hejaz U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Hejaz)___ .
Ibn Saud avoided involvement in the Arab Revolt and instead continued his struggle with the Al Rashid.

Following the latter's final defeat, he took the title ___E:Sultan of Nejd U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sultanate_of_Nejd)___ in 1921. With the help of the Ikhwan, the Kingdom of Hejaz was conquered in 1924–25, and on 10 January 1926, Ibn Saud declared himself king of Hejaz.
For the next five years, he administered the two parts of his dual kingdom as separate units.

After the conquest of the Hejaz, the Ikhwan leadership's objective switched to expansion of the Wahhabist realm into the British protectorates of Transjordan, Iraq and Kuwait, and began raiding those territories.
This met with Ibn Saud's opposition, as he recognized the danger of a direct conflict with the British.
At the same time, the Ikhwan became disenchanted with Ibn Saud's domestic policies which appeared to favour modernization and the increase in the number of non-Muslim foreigners in the country.

As a result, they turned against Ibn Saud and, after a two-year struggle, were defeated in 1929 at the ___E:Battle of Sabilla U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Sabilla)___ , where their leaders were massacred.

On Ibn Saud's behalf, ___E:Prince Faisal U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_bin_Abdulaziz_al_Saud)___ declared the unification on 23 September 1932, and the two kingdoms of Hejaz and Nejd were unified as the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia.
That date is now a national holiday called ___E:Saudi National Day U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi_National_Day)___ .

The new kingdom was reliant on limited agriculture and pilgrimage revenues.  ___E:In 1938, vast reserves of oil were discovered U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dammam_No._7)___ in the Al-Ahsa region along the coast of the Persian Gulf, and full-scale development of the oil fields began in 1941 under the US-controlled ___E:Aramco (Arabian American Oil Company) U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi_Aramco)___ .
Oil provided Saudi Arabia with economic prosperity and substantial political leverage internationally.
Cultural life rapidly developed, primarily in the Hejaz, which was the centre for newspapers and radio.

However, the large influx of ___E:foreign workers in Saudi Arabia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign_workers_in_Saudi_Arabia)___ in the oil industry increased the pre-existing propensity for ___E:xenophobia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xenophobia)___ .
At the same time, the government became increasingly wasteful and extravagant.
By the 1950s this had led to large governmental deficits and excessive foreign borrowing.
In 1953, ___E:Saud of Saudi Arabia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saud_of_Saudi_Arabia)___ succeeded as the king of Saudi Arabia.

In 1964 he was deposed in favour of his half brother ___E:Faisal of Saudi Arabia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_of_Saudi_Arabia)___ , after an intense rivalry, fuelled by doubts in the royal family over Saud's competence.

In 1972, Saudi Arabia gained a 20% control in Aramco, thereby decreasing US control over Saudi oil.  In 1973, Saudi Arabia led an ___E:oil boycott U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1973_oil_crisis)___ against the Western countries that supported Israel in the ___E:Yom Kippur War U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yom_Kippur_War)___ against Egypt and Syria, leading to the quadrupling of oil prices.

In 1975, Faisal was assassinated by his nephew, Prince ___E:Faisal bin Musaid U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_bin_Musaid)___ and was succeeded by his half-brother ___E:King Khalid U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khalid_of_Saudi_Arabia)___ .
By 1976, Saudi Arabia had become the largest oil producer in the world.

Khalid's reign saw economic and social development progress at an extremely rapid rate, transforming the infrastructure and educational system of the country;  in foreign policy, close ties with the US were developed.
In 1979, two events occurred which greatly concerned the government  and had a long-term influence on Saudi foreign and domestic policy.
The first was the ___E:Iranian Islamic Revolution U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iranian_Revolution)___ .

It was feared that the country's ___E:Shi'ite minority U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shi%27a_Islam_in_Saudi_Arabia)___ in the Eastern Province (which is also the location of the oil fields) might rebel under the influence of their Iranian co-religionists.
There were several anti-government uprisings in the region such as the ___E:1979 Qatif Uprising U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1979_Qatif_Uprising)___ .
The second event was the ___E:Grand Mosque Seizure U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Mosque_Seizure)___ in Mecca by Islamist extremists.
The militants involved were in part angered by what they considered to be the corruption and un-Islamic nature of the Saudi government.
The government regained control of the mosque after 10 days, and those captured were executed.

Part of the response of the royal family was to enforce the much stricter observance of traditional religious and social norms in the country (for example, the closure of cinemas) and to give the ___E:ulema U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulema)___ a greater role in government.
Neither entirely succeeded as Islamism continued to grow in strength.
In 1980, Saudi Arabia bought out the American interests in Aramco.

King Khalid died of a heart attack in June 1982. He was succeeded by his brother, ___E:King Fahd U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fahd_of_Saudi_Arabia)___ , who added the title "Custodian of the Two Holy Mosques" to his name in 1986 in response to considerable fundamentalist pressure to avoid the use of "majesty" in association with anything except God. Fahd continued to develop close relations with the United States and increased the purchase of American and British military equipment.
The vast wealth generated by oil revenues was beginning to have an even greater impact on Saudi society.
It led to rapid technological (but not cultural) modernization, urbanization, mass public education, and the creation of new media.
This and the presence of increasingly large numbers of foreign workers greatly affected traditional Saudi norms and values.

Although there was a dramatic change in the social and economic life of the country, political power continued to be monopolized by the royal family  leading to discontent among many Saudis who began to look for wider participation in government.

In the 1980s, Saudi Arabia and ___E:Kuwait U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kuwait)___ spent $25 billion in support of ___E:Saddam Hussein U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saddam_Hussein)___ in the ___E:Iran–Iraq War U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iran%E2%80%93Iraq_War)___ (1980–1988);  however, Saudi Arabia condemned the ___E:invasion of Kuwait U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Invasion_of_Kuwait)___ in 1990 and asked the United States to intervene.
King Fahd allowed American and coalition troops to be stationed in Saudi Arabia.

He invited the Kuwaiti government and many of its citizens to stay in Saudi Arabia, but expelled citizens of ___E:Yemen U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yemen)___ and ___E:Jordan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jordan)___ because of their governments' support of ___E:Iraq U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ba%27athist_Iraq)___ .

In 1991, Saudi Arabian forces were involved both in bombing raids on Iraq and in the land invasion that helped to liberate Kuwait, which became known as the ___E:Gulf War U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_War)___ (1990–1991).

Saudi Arabia's relations with the West was one of the issues that led to ___E:an increase in Islamist terrorism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_militant_incidents_in_Saudi_Arabia)___ in Saudi Arabia, as well as Islamist terrorist attacks in Western countries by Saudi nationals. ___E:Osama bin Laden U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osama_bin_Laden)___ was a Saudi citizen (until stripped of his citizenship in 1994) and was responsible for the ___E:1998 U.S. embassy bombings U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998_United_States_embassy_bombings)___ in East Africa and the 2000 ___E:USS Cole bombing U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Cole_bombing)___ near the port of ___E:Aden U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aden)___ , Yemen. 15 of ___E:the hijackers U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hijackers_in_the_September_11_attacks)___ involved in the ___E:September 11 attacks U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/September_11_attacks)___ were Saudi nationals.
Many Saudis who did not support the Islamist terrorists were nevertheless deeply unhappy with the government's policies.
Islamism was not the only source of hostility to the government.
Although extremely wealthy by the 21st century, Saudi Arabia's economy was near stagnant.
High taxes and a growth in unemployment have contributed to discontent and have been reflected in a rise in civil unrest, and discontent with the royal family.

In response, a number of limited reforms were initiated by King Fahd. In March 1992, he introduced the " ___E:Basic Law U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basic_Law_of_Saudi_Arabia)___ ", which emphasized the duties and responsibilities of a ruler.
In December 1993, the Consultative Council was inaugurated.

It is composed of a chairman and 60 members—all chosen by the King. Fahd made it clear that he did not have democracy in mind, saying: "A system based on elections is not consistent with our Islamic creed, which [approves of] government by consultation [shūrā]."

In 1995, Fahd suffered a debilitating stroke, and the Crown Prince, ___E:Abdullah U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abdullah_of_Saudi_Arabia)___ , assumed the role of de facto regent; however, his authority was hindered by conflict with Fahd's full brothers (known, with Fahd, as the " ___E:Sudairi Seven U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sudairi_Seven)___ ").
Signs of discontent included, in 2003 and 2004, a series of bombings and armed violence in Riyadh, Jeddah, Yanbu and Khobar.
In February–April 2005, ___E:the first-ever nationwide municipal elections U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2005_Saudi_Arabian_municipal_elections)___ were held in Saudi Arabia.
Women were not allowed to take part.
In 2005, King Fahd died and was succeeded by Abdullah, who continued the policy of minimum reform and clamping down on protests.

The king introduced economic reforms aimed at reducing the country's reliance on oil revenue: limited ___E:deregulation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deregulation)___ , encouragement of foreign investment, and ___E:privatization U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Privatization)___ .

In February 2009, Abdullah announced a series of governmental changes to the judiciary, armed forces, and various ministries to modernize these institutions including the replacement of senior appointees in the judiciary and the ___E:Mutaween U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_religious_police)___ (religious police) with more moderate individuals and the appointment of the country's first female deputy minister.

On 29 January 2011, hundreds of protesters gathered in ___E:Jeddah U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeddah)___ in a rare display of criticism against the city's poor infrastructure after flooding killed 11 people.
Police stopped the demonstration after about 15 minutes and arrested 30 to 50 people.
Since 2011, Saudi Arabia has been affected by its own ___E:Arab Spring protests U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011%E2%80%9313_Saudi_Arabian_protests)___ .
In response, King Abdullah announced on 22 February 2011 a series of benefits for citizens amounting to $36 billion, of which $10.7 billion was earmarked for housing.
No political reforms were included, though some prisoners indicted for financial crimes were pardoned.

Abdullah also announced a package of $93 billion, which included 500,000 new homes to a cost of $67 billion, in addition to creating 60000 new security jobs.   Although male-only ___E:municipal elections were held on 29 September 2011 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi_Arabian_municipal_elections,_2011)___ ,   Abdullah allowed women to vote and be elected in the ___E:2015 municipal elections U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi_Arabian_municipal_elections,_2015)___ , and also to be nominated to the ___E:Shura Council U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consultative_Assembly_of_Saudi_Arabia)___ .

Saudi Arabia occupies about 80% of the ___E:Arabian Peninsula U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabian_Peninsula)___ (the world's largest peninsula),  lying between latitudes ___E:16° U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/16th_parallel_north)___ and ___E:33° N U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/33rd_parallel_north)___ , and longitudes ___E:34° U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/34th_meridian_east)___ and ___E:56° E U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/56th_meridian_east)___ .

Because the country's southeastern and southern borders with the ___E:United Arab Emirates U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates)___ and ___E:Oman U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oman)___ are not precisely marked, the exact size of the country is undefined.

The ___E:United Nations Statistics Division U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Statistics_Division)___ estimates 2149690 km 2 ( 830000 sq mi) and lists Saudi Arabia as the world's ___E:12th U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_and_dependencies_by_area)___ largest state.
It is geographically the largest country in the Middle East and on the ___E:Arabian Plate U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabian_Plate)___ .

Saudi Arabia's geography is dominated by the ___E:Arabian Desert U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabian_Desert)___ , associated semi-desert, shrubland, steppes, several mountain ranges, volcanic lava fields and highlands.

The 647500 km 2 ( 250001 sq mi) ___E:Rub' al Khali U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rub%27_al_Khali)___ ("Empty Quarter") in the southeastern part of the country is the world's largest contiguous sand desert.

Though there are lakes in the country, Saudi Arabia is the largest country in the world by area with no permanent rivers. ___E:Wadis U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wadis)___ , non-permanent rivers, however, ___E:are very numerous throughout the kingdom U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_wadis_of_Saudi_Arabia)___ .
The fertile areas are to be found in the alluvial deposits in wadis, basins, and oases.
There are ___E:approximately 1,300 islands U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_islands_of_Saudi_Arabia)___ in the Red Sea and Persian Gulf.

The main topographical feature is the central plateau which rises abruptly from the Red Sea and gradually descends into the ___E:Nejd U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nejd)___ and toward the Persian Gulf. On the Red Sea coast, there is a narrow coastal plain, known as the ___E:Tihamah U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tihamah)___ , parallel to which runs along an imposing escarpment.

The southwest province of ___E:Aseer U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aseer)___ is mountainous and contains the 3002 m ( 9849 ft) ___E:Jabal Ferwa U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jabal_Ferwa_(Asir))___ , which is the highest point in the country.
Saudi Arabia is home to more than 2,000 dormant volcanoes.

Lava fields in Hejaz, known locally by their Arabic name of harrat (the singular is harrah), form one of Earth's largest ___E:alkali basalt U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alkali_basalt)___ regions, covering some 180,000 square kilometres (69,000 sq mi).

Except for the southwestern regions such as Aseer, Saudi Arabia has a ___E:desert climate U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desert_climate)___ with very high day-time temperatures during the summer and a sharp temperature drop at night.
Average summer temperatures are around 45 °C (113 °F) but can be as high as 54 °C (129 °F).

In the winter the temperature rarely drops below 0 °C (32 °F) with the exception of mostly the northern regions of the country where annual snowfall, in particular in the mountainous regions of ___E:Tabuk Province U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tabuk_Province)___ , is not uncommon.
The lowest recorded temperature, −12.0 °C (10.4 °F), was measured in ___E:Turaif U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turaif)___ .
Of the Gulf states, Saudi Arabia is likely to experience snowfalls most frequently.
In the spring and autumn the heat is temperate, temperatures average around 29 °C (84 °F).

Annual rainfall is very low. The southern regions differ in that they are influenced by the Indian Ocean ___E:monsoons U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monsoons)___ , usually occurring between October and March.
An average of 300 mm (12 in) of rainfall occurs during this period, which is about 60% of the annual precipitation.

Saudi Arabia is home to five terrestrial ecoregions: ___E:Arabian Peninsula coastal fog desert U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabian_Peninsula_coastal_fog_desert)___ , ___E:Southwestern Arabian foothills savanna U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southwestern_Arabian_foothills_savanna)___ , ___E:Southwestern Arabian montane woodlands U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southwestern_Arabian_montane_woodlands)___ , ___E:Arabian Desert U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabian_Desert)___ , and ___E:Red Sea Nubo-Sindian tropical desert and semi-desert U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Sea_Nubo-Sindian_tropical_desert_and_semi-desert)___ .

Wildlife includes the ___E:Arabian leopard U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabian_leopard)___ ,   ___E:Arabian wolf U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabian_wolf)___ , ___E:striped hyena U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Striped_hyena)___ , ___E:mongoose U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mongoose)___ , ___E:baboon U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baboon)___ , ___E:Cape hare U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_hare)___ , ___E:sand cat U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sand_cat)___ , and ___E:jerboa U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerboa)___ .

Animals such as gazelles, ___E:oryx U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oryx)___ , leopards and ___E:cheetahs U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asiatic_cheetah)___  were relatively numerous until the 19th century, when extensive hunting reduced these animals almost to extinction.

The culturally important ___E:Asiatic lion U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asiatic_lion)___ occurred in Saudi Arabia until the late 19th century before it was hunted to extinction in the wild.  Birds include falcons (which are caught and trained for hunting), eagles, hawks, vultures, ___E:sandgrouse U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandgrouse)___ , and ___E:bulbuls U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulbul)___ .
There are several species of snakes, many of which are venomous.

Domesticated animals include the legendary ___E:Arabian horse U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabian_horse)___ , ___E:Arabian camel U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabian_camel)___ , sheep, goats, cattle, donkeys, chickens, etc.

The Red Sea is a rich and diverse ___E:ecosystem U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecosystem)___ with more than ___E:1,200 species of fish U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_fishes_in_the_Red_Sea)___  around 10% of which are ___E:endemic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endemism)___ .
This also includes 42 species of ___E:deep water fish U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_deep_water_fish_of_the_Red_Sea)___ .

The rich diversity is partly owed to the 2000 km ( 1240 mi) of coral reef extending along the coastline; these ___E:fringing reefs U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fringing_reef)___ are largely formed of stony ___E:acropora U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acropora)___ and ___E:porites U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porites)___ corals.

The reefs form platforms and sometimes lagoons along the coast and occasional other features such as cylinders (such as the ___E:Blue Hole U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Hole_(Red_Sea))___ at ___E:Dahab U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dahab)___ ).

These coastal reefs are also visited by ___E:pelagic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pelagic_zone)___ species, including some of the ___E:44 species of shark U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_sharks_in_the_Red_Sea)___ .
There are many offshore reefs including several ___E:atolls U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atoll)___ .

Many of the unusual offshore reef formations defy classic (i.e., Darwinian) coral reef classification schemes and are generally attributed to the high levels of tectonic activity that characterize the area.
Reflecting the country's dominant desert conditions, plant life mostly consists of herbs, plants, and shrubs that require little water.
The date palm ( Phoenix dactylifera ) is widespread.

Saudi Arabia is an ___E:absolute monarchy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Absolute_monarchy)___ ;  however, according to the ___E:Basic Law of Saudi Arabia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basic_Law_of_Saudi_Arabia)___ adopted by royal decree in 1992, the king must comply with ___E:Sharia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sharia)___ (Islamic law) and the ___E:Quran U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quran)___ , while the Quran and the ___E:Sunnah U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunnah)___ (the traditions of Muhammad) are declared to be the country's constitution.
No political parties or national elections are permitted.

While some critics consider it to be a ___E:totalitarian U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Totalitarianism)___ state,   others regard it as lacking aspects of totalitarianism but nevertheless classify it as an authoritarian regime.

The Economist ranked the Saudi government 150th out of 167 in its 2022 ___E:Democracy Index U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democracy_Index)___ ,  and ___E:Freedom House U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_House)___ gave it its lowest "Not Free" rating, giving it a score of 8 out of 100 for 2023.  According to the 2023 ___E:V-Dem Democracy Indices U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V-Dem_Democracy_Indices)___ , Saudi Arabia is the least ___E:democratic country in the Middle East U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democracy_in_the_Middle_East_and_North_Africa)___ .

Additionally, according to ___E:International IDEA U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Institute_for_Democracy_and_Electoral_Assistance)___ ’s Global State of Democracy (GSoD) Indices and Democracy Tracker, Saudi Arabia performs in the low range on overall democratic measures, with particular weaknesses in political representation, including credible elections, inclusive suffrage and effective parliament.

In the absence of national elections and political parties,  politics in Saudi Arabia takes place in two distinct arenas: within the royal family, the Al Saud, and between the royal family and the rest of Saudi society.

Outside of the Al Saud, participation in the political process is limited to a relatively small segment of the population and takes the form of the royal family consulting with the ulema, tribal sheikhs, and members of important commercial families on major decisions.
This process is not reported by the Saudi media.
By custom, all males of full age have a right to petition the king directly through the traditional tribal meeting known as the majlis .

In many ways the approach to government differs little from the traditional system of tribal rule. Tribal identity remains strong, and outside of the royal family, political influence is frequently determined by tribal affiliation, with tribal sheikhs maintaining a considerable degree of influence over local and national events.

In recent years there have been limited steps to widen political participation such as the establishment of the Consultative Council in the early 1990s and the National Dialogue Forum in 2003.  In 2005, the first municipal elections were held. In 2007, the ___E:Allegiance Council U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allegiance_Council)___ was created to regulate the succession.

In 2009, the king made significant personnel changes to the government by appointing reformers to key positions and the first woman to a ministerial post;   however, these changes have been criticized as being too slow or merely cosmetic.

The rule of the Al Saud faces political opposition from four sources: Sunni Islamist activism; liberal critics; the ___E:Shi'ite minority U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shia_Islam_in_Saudi_Arabia)___ —particularly in the Eastern Province; and long-standing tribal and ___E:regionalist U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regionalism_(politics))___ particularistic opponents (for example in the Hejaz).

Of these, the minority activists have been the most prominent threat to the government and have in recent years been involved in ___E:violent incidents in the country U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_terrorist_incidents_in_Saudi_Arabia)___ .
However, open protest against the government, even if peaceful, is not tolerated.
The king combines legislative, executive, and judicial functions  and royal decrees form the basis of the country's legislation.

The prime minister presides over the ___E:Council of Ministers of Saudi Arabia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_of_Ministers_of_Saudi_Arabia)___ and ___E:Consultative Assembly of Saudi Arabia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consultative_Assembly_of_Saudi_Arabia)___ .

The king has usually been also the prime minister, with two exceptions: Crown Prince ___E:Faisal U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_of_Saudi_Arabia)___ , who was prime minister during the reign of ___E:King Saud U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saud_of_Saudi_Arabia)___ ,  and Crown Prince ___E:Mohammed Bin Salman U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_Bin_Salman)___ , the current prime minister since 2022.  The royal family dominates the political system.
The family's vast numbers allows it to control most of the kingdom's important posts and to have an involvement and presence at all levels of government.

The number of princes is estimated to be at least 7000 , with most power and influence being wielded by the 200 or so male descendants of Ibn Saud.  The key ministries are generally reserved for the royal family,  as are the 13 regional governorships.
The Saudi government    and the royal family    have often been accused of corruption over many years,  and this continues into the 21st century.
In a country that is said to "belong" to the royal family and is named for them,  the lines between state assets and the personal wealth of senior princes are blurred.

The extent of corruption has been described as systemic  and endemic,  and its existence was acknowledged  and defended  by ___E:Prince Bandar bin Sultan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bandar_bin_Sultan)___ (a senior member of the royal family)  in an interview in 2001.

Saudi Arabia has undergone a process of political and social reform, such as to increase public transparency and good governance, but nepotism and patronage are widespread when doing business in the country; the enforcement of the anti-corruption laws is selective and public officials engage in corruption with impunity.

As many as 500 people, including prominent Saudi Arabian princes, government ministers, and businesspeople, were ___E:arrested in an anti-corruption campaign U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017%E2%80%932019_Saudi_Arabian_purge)___ in November 2017.
Saudi Arabia is unique in giving the ___E:ulema U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulama)___ (the body of Islamic religious leaders and jurists) a direct role in government.
The preferred ulema are of the ___E:Salafi movement U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salafi_movement)___ .

The ulema have been a key influence in major government decisions, for example the imposition of the ___E:oil embargo in 1973 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1973_oil_crisis)___ and the ___E:invitation to foreign troops to Saudi Arabia in 1990 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_War)___ .
In addition, they have had a major role in the judicial and education systems  and a monopoly of authority in religious and social morals.
By the 1970s, as a result of oil wealth and the modernization initiated by King Faisal, important changes to Saudi society were underway, and the power of the ulema was in decline.
However, this changed following the ___E:seizure of the Grand Mosque U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Mosque_seizure)___ in Mecca in 1979 by Islamist radicals.

The government's response to the crisis included strengthening the ulema's powers and increasing their financial support:  in particular, they were given greater control over the education system  and allowed to enforce the stricter observance of Wahhabi rules of moral and social behaviour.
After his accession to the throne in 2005, King Abdullah took steps to reduce the powers of the ulema, for instance transferring control over girls' education to the Ministry of Education.
The ulema have historically been led by the ___E:Al ash-Sheikh U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_ash-Sheikh)___ ,  the country's leading religious family.

The Al ash-Sheikh are the descendants of ___E:Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_ibn_Abd_al-Wahhab)___ , the 18th-century founder of the Wahhabi form of Sunni Islam which is today dominant in Saudi Arabia.

The family is second in prestige only to the Al Saud (the royal family)  with whom they formed a "mutual support pact"  and power-sharing arrangement nearly 300 years ago.  The pact, which persists to this day,  is based on the Al Saud maintaining the Al ash-Sheikh's authority in religious matters and upholding and propagating Wahhabi doctrine.

In return, the Al ash-Sheikh support the Al Saud's political authority  thereby using its religious- ___E:moral authority U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moral_authority)___ to legitimize the royal family's rule.  Although the Al ash-Sheikh's domination of the ulema has diminished in recent decades,  they still hold the most important religious posts and are closely linked to the Al Saud by a high degree of intermarriage.

The primary source of law is the Islamic ___E:Sharia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sharia)___ derived from the teachings of the ___E:Qur'an U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qur%27an)___ and the ___E:Sunnah U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunnah)___ (the traditions of the Prophet).
Saudi Arabia is unique among modern Muslim states in that Sharia is not codified and there is no system of judicial precedent, allowing judges to use independent legal reasoning to make a decision.
Thus, divergent judgments arise even in apparently identical cases,  making predictability of legal interpretation difficult.

Saudi judges tend to follow the principles of the ___E:Hanbali U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hanbali)___ ___E:school of jurisprudence U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madhhab)___ ( fiqh ) found in pre-modern texts and noted for its literalist interpretation of the Qur'an and ___E:hadith U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hadith)___ .
In 2021, Saudi Arabia announced judicial reforms to entirely ___E:codify its laws U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codification_(law))___ and eliminate discrepancies.
Royal decrees are the other main source of law but are referred to as regulations rather than laws because they are subordinate to Sharia.
Royal decrees supplement Sharia in areas such as labour, commercial and corporate law. Additionally, traditional tribal law and custom remain significant.
Extra-Sharia government tribunals usually handle disputes relating to specific royal decrees.
Final appeal from both Sharia courts and government tribunals is to the king, and all courts and tribunals follow Sharia rules of evidence and procedure.

Retaliatory punishments, or ___E:Qisas U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qisas)___ , are practised: for instance, an eye can be surgically removed at the insistence of a victim who lost his own eye.  Families of someone unlawfully killed can choose between demanding the death penalty or granting clemency in return for a payment of ___E:diyya U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diyya)___ (blood money), by the perpetrator.

Saudi Arabia is divided into 13 ___E:regions U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regions)___  ( ___E:Arabic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabic_language)___ : مناطق إدارية ; manatiq idāriyya , sing. منطقة إدارية; mintaqah idariyya ).

The regions are further divided into 118 ___E:governorates U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governorates_of_Saudi_Arabia)___ ( ___E:Arabic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabic_language)___ : محافظات ; muhafazat , sing. محافظة; muhafazah ).

This number includes the 13 regional capitals, which have a different status as municipalities ( ___E:Arabic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabic_language)___ : أمانة ; amanah ) headed by mayors ( ___E:Arabic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabic_language)___ : أمين ; amin ).
The governorates are further subdivided into sub-governorates ( ___E:Arabic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabic_language)___ : مراكز ; marakiz , sing. مركز; markaz ).

The foreign policy of Saudi Arabia is officially focused on cooperation with the oil-exporting ___E:Gulf States U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arab_states_of_the_Persian_Gulf)___ , the unity of the ___E:Arab world U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arab_World)___ , ___E:Islamic solidarity U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ummah)___ , and support for the ___E:United Nations U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations)___ and multilateralism.

The embargo caused an ___E:oil crisis U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1973_oil_crisis)___ with many short- and long-term effects on global politics and the global economy.

___E:Saudi Arabia and the United States U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi_Arabia%E2%80%93United_States_relations)___ are strategic allies;    the U.S. has been the most influential foreign power in the kingdom since the end of World War II. The ___E:Armed Forces of Saudi Arabia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armed_Forces_of_Saudi_Arabia)___ are under the ___E:Ministry of Defence U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Defence_(Saudi_Arabia))___ and consist of the ___E:Royal Saudi Land Forces U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi_Arabian_Army)___ (including the ___E:Royal Guard U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi_Royal_Guard_Regiment)___ ), the ___E:Air Force U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Saudi_Air_Force)___ , the ___E:Navy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Saudi_Navy)___ , the ___E:Air Defence U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Saudi_Air_Defense_Forces)___ , and the ___E:Strategic Missile Force U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Saudi_Strategic_Missile_Force)___ ; the ___E:Saudi Arabian National Guard U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi_Arabian_National_Guard)___ , which is under the ___E:Ministry of National Guard U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_National_Guard)___ , is made up of tribal forces loyal to the Saudi royal family and plays a role in both domestic security and foreign defence.

The Saudi government, which mandates Muslim and non-Muslim observance of Sharia law under the absolute rule of the House of Saud, has been denounced by international organizations and governments for violating human rights.

The authoritarian regime is consistently ranked among the "worst of the worst" in ___E:Freedom House U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_House)___ 's ___E:annual survey of political and civil rights U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_in_the_World)___ .

Mass executions, such as those carried out ___E:in 2016 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Saudi_Arabia_mass_execution)___  and ___E:2019 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_Saudi_Arabia_mass_execution)___  and ___E:2022 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Saudi_Arabia_mass_execution)___  have been condemned by international rights groups.

Saudi Arabian law does not recognize ___E:sexual orientations U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LGBT_rights_in_Saudi_Arabia)___ or religious freedom, and the public practice of non-Muslim religions is actively prohibited.

The justice system regularly engages in ___E:capital punishment U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_punishment)___ , which has included public executions by ___E:decapitation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decapitation)___ .
